To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have synthesized and characterized a new family of IR-emitting QDs that can be used for tissue imaging, and have shown that DNA can be used to stabilize them and direct their assembly into nanostructured materials.
we produced Cd(x)Pd(1-x)T QDs that emit IR light and are stable in high salt solutions.
we synthesized IR-emitting quantum dots (QDs) that emit in the wavelength range of 1100- 1300 nm, and we showed that DNA can be used to conjugate to QD surfaces.
In summary, our research is concerned with
producing QDs that can be conjugated to specific surface tags, and can be directed to self-assemble onto nanostructures, in order to achieve the desired functionality.
the production of QDs with tunable emission in the IR region of the spectrum and the use of DNA to direct their assembly into nanostructures.
the synthesis and characterization of QDs, their DNA functionalization, and their assembly on DNA nanostructures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the QD-DNA conjugates can be assembled onto a DNA origami template and the resulting structures can be imaged using confocal microscopy.
the ligand identity has a profound impact on the optical properties of the resulting QDs.
the ligand used in the synthesis affects the Cd/Pb ratio of the particles and thus the emission wavelength of the particle.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have successfully developed a facile, one-pot synthesis of IR-emitting QDs with tunable emission wavelengths and demonstrated their conjugation with DNA, which is a necessary step for their biological applications.
we have successfully produced IR QDs with DNA surface tags, and have demonstrated that these QDs can be assembled on a DNA origami nanostructure.
we have produced IR emitting QDs that can be functionalized with DNA for specific targeting and that these particles can be self-assembled into DNA origami nanostructures for use as scaffolds.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the ligand used to cap the QDs can influence the particle composition and thus the emission peak of the particles, and that DNA directed assembly is a viable approach to stabilizing QDs in the presence of high salt.

the surface chemistry of these particles can be tuned to achieve desired emission peaks, and DNA conjugation and assembly can be used to stabilize the particles for biological applications.
